title: Ask the Buddha
hookLine: a monk climbs through the heavens asking where the elements end; the great Brahma draws him aside and says ask the Buddha
carry: the answer was back on the ground
tomorrow: Where the elements find no footing

cards: It begins with a request for a show. A householder named Kevaddha comes to the Buddha in Nalanda. This town is prosperous, he says, and full of people who trust you.
If one of your monks would just perform a miracle, they'd trust you even more. The Buddha says no. Three times Kevaddha asks, and three times, no.
Then the Buddha explains. There are three kinds of wonder: the wonder of psychic power, the wonder of reading minds, and the wonder of instruction.

teach.b: Flying through the air, walking on water: a skeptic, the Buddha says, would just say it's done with a charm. Reading minds: the same. So he finds those wonders troubling, and doesn't trade on them.
The real wonder is instruction, a teaching that changes how someone lives. The Pali word is patihariya: wonder, marvel. Then, to show what instruction means, a story.
Once a monk wondered: where do the four great elements, earth, water, fire and air, cease without remainder? He entered deep meditation and went to ask the gods.
The gods of the Four Great Kings said: we don't know, ask the Thirty-Three. They said: ask Sakka.
Sakka said: ask the next heaven up. Higher and higher, until the gods of Brahma's company said: we don't know, but the great Brahma will. The great Brahma appears.
I am Brahma, the great Brahma, the all-seeing, the lord. I didn't ask who you are, says the monk. I asked where the elements cease.
The third time, Brahma takes the monk by the arm, leads him aside, and says quietly: these gods think there's nothing I don't know. That's why I didn't answer in front of them.
But I don't know. You did wrong to pass over the Blessed One and come looking up here. Go back and ask him.
In this Buddhist story, Brahma is honest at last, in private.
Hindu traditions understand Brahma in their own ways; the story's own point is about the monk, who climbed through every heaven, when the answer was back on the ground.

how: Many Buddhist teachers cite this discourse to say that the true marvel is teaching that transforms people, and Buddhist monastic rules forbid monks from displaying psychic powers to lay people.

o: a magic charm said over the sick
a prayer sent up to the heavens

games.q: ask the Buddha: tap the pairs.
p: asked for a miracle in Nalanda

s: the Buddha agrees to have a monk perform a miracle for the town
he refuses three times and explains the three kinds of wonder.
the monk is passed from heaven to heaven, each saying ask higher
until he reaches the great Brahma.
the great Brahma admits his ignorance in front of all the gods
he takes the monk aside, so the gods won't hear, and says: I don't know, go ask the Buddha.

games.q: you're the great Brahma. a monk asks where the four elements cease, and you don't know. all your gods are watching. what do you do?
o: take him aside and admit it privately.
send him to a lower heaven.
games.why: twice Brahma just repeats his titles. the third time he takes the monk by the arm, leads him aside, admits he doesn't know, and sends him back to the Buddha.

practice: Think of a question you've been carrying, about work, health or a relationship, and notice who you've been asking: people who sound impressive, maybe, or the internet at 2am.
Then ask who actually knows, someone close by with real experience whom you've been passing over, and picture asking them plainly.

wordCard.voice: Patihariya. The wonder of instruction: a monk climbs through every heaven, and the great Brahma takes him aside and sends him back to the one who knows.

orig.note: Pali patihariya: wonder, marvel. the three: psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction.

carryVoice: Your line: the answer was back on the ground. The real wonder was a teaching, not a show. Day five hundred thirty-eight, done.
